revisions.text: Dark tea is made to be kept, and the trade values it more with age. Over years it turns darker and redder in the cup and grows mellower and sweeter. How fast it changes depends on how it is stored, and the trade does not agree on one way: some keep it cool and dry for a slow, clean change, others warmer and more humid for a faster, deeper one. When a tea counts as young or aged differs from style to style, so each style sets its own measure.

Dark tea takes boiling water. Its leaf is mature and dense, so it gives up its flavour slowly and is hard to overbrew. Rinse it first with boiling water and pour that off within seconds: the rinse wakes the leaf and washes off dust and any stale smell from storage, and an old tea may take a second rinse. In a small pot use plenty of leaf, about 7 grams to 120 ml, then steep very briefly at first and a little longer each time; a good dark tea gives many cups.

From a brick, cake or basket, ease the leaf off along the edge or from the top with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole pieces give up their flavour steadily; crumbs release it all at once and cloud the cup.

Older or coarse dark tea is often simmered rather than steeped: the leaf goes into a pot of water, comes to a gentle boil and simmers for a few minutes. Thick leaf and long-aged tea release their flavour slowly, and the steady heat gives a fuller, smoother cup than short steeps do.

A smooth, mellow cup with low bitterness and a deep red colour, often sweet and woody or earthy, sometimes with herbal or medicinal notes. A young dark tea can still smell of the pile or of storage; an aged one is usually redder, sweeter and thicker.

Dark tea is Chinese tea whose leaf, after it is heated and rolled, is left to change in warmth and moisture, where microbes and the leaf’s own chemistry slowly darken and mellow it. Because that change comes after the leaf is made, the trade calls it post-fermented. In Chinese it is hei cha, “black tea”, which is not the English black tea; that tea is red tea, hong cha, in Chinese.

The first records of dark tea by name are from the Ming dynasty, in Hunan around Anhua and in Sichuan, and in the late Ming it became a state-managed tea sent to the north-west in exchange for horses. In the Qing dynasty merchants carried the craft to more regions and more shapes, and some styles were made for new markets: Guangxi’s Liu Bao, for one, went to the tin mines of Southeast Asia. In the twentieth century state factories took over much of the making and settled the brick shapes that are sold today.

Most dark tea shares four steps, each with a reason. The leaf is heated first, the kill-green, to stop its own enzymes from browning it; coarse leaf is often sprinkled with a little water so it heats evenly. It is rolled gently, because the large, mature leaf used for dark tea is tough and breaks if it is worked hard. It is then piled, and in the pile warmth, moisture and microbes do the darkening and mellowing, so the heap is turned to keep its heat in range. Finally it is dried, which stops the change and makes the tea stable enough to keep. Many styles then steam the leaf and press it, or pack it into baskets, and let it age.

Dark tea was made for people who lived far from where tea grows: Tibet, Mongolia, China’s north-west and, later, Central Asia and Russia. The trade called it border tea. The tea had to survive months on the road, so it was pressed into bricks, cakes and logs, or packed tight in baskets. A dense, even shape is easier to carry, stack and strap to a pack animal, and it keeps better than loose leaf. Some dark tea is still sold loose.

Greater Yiwu is often associated with a softer opening and a persistent sweet return when compared with the more forceful profiles linked to western Xishuangbanna. The area contains many growing places, however, and their material can vary substantially; this is a regional tendency, not a tasting promise for an individual tea.

Yiwu became an important collection and distribution point for tea from the old Six Famous Tea Mountains. Its trade connected local leaf, merchant networks, tribute routes, and later some of the best-known early twentieth-century tea firms.

Yiwu can mean a township, a market center, or a much broader tea area in eastern Xishuangbanna. In trade, the name often reaches beyond the town itself, so a Yiwu label should be read as a regional claim whose scale still needs context.

Young single-origin Lincang sheng is often described as green, firm, and bitter. This reputation is useful as a starting point only: Lincang is a large prefecture, and material from its counties, mountains, and villages should not be collapsed into one tasting profile.

Lincang has a smaller public archive of famous aged single-origin teas than Yiwu or Menghai. Older blended productions, especially those associated with Xiaguan, nevertheless provide a historical thread, even when the exact origin of their base material cannot be reconstructed.

Lincang lies north of Pu’er Prefecture and against Myanmar to the west. Its tea geography includes Mengku, Yongde, Fengqing, Bangdong, Bingdao, and Xigui, with repeated place names such as Daxueshan making precise labels especially important.

After about ten years the trade counts a Liu Bao as aged. The cup turns amber to deep red-brown, thick and smooth, with woody and herbal notes, and decades-old tea is often said to take on ginseng and camphor. How it was stored matters as much as how long, and the trade does not agree whether it keeps improving for decades or peaks sooner.
Between about five and ten years the aged character begins to show. The pile smell has gone, the cup deepens toward red, and the woody, sweet notes the trade looks for start to come through.
Under about five years a Liu Bao is still young. Its cup is paler, yellow to orange, and it can carry a faint smell of the pile and a little brightness or bitterness that age will soften.

Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.
A sweet, smooth cup, woody and herbal, which the trade sums up as red, thick, aged and mellow. The note most often named is betel nut, faint in younger tea and clearer with age.

Liu Bao is a dark tea from Cangwu County, near Wuzhou in Guangxi, named for the town of Liubao where it began. Like every dark tea, its leaf is piled after it is made, so that warmth, moisture and microbes turn it darker and softer, and then it is packed and left to age.

From the late 1930s war and blockade cut the river trade, and in the decades that followed production fell further as the planned economy changed who could buy and sell tea, and later as farmers left tea for other work. When the Malaysian tin mines declined, much old stock was left sitting in warehouses in Malaysia and Hong Kong. That forgotten stock is where most very old Liu Bao comes from today.

In the 1950s the Wuzhou tea factory worked out cold-water piling, around 1958: the leaf is wetted and heaped at a modest warmth and turned until it has darkened, a steadier route than the farmhouse steaming. Factory tea, too, is packed in baskets and aged before sale.

The older, farmhouse way of making Liu Bao leans on steam and time. The leaf is steamed to soften it, then heaped damp so it darkens and loses its bitterness, and in most accounts it is steamed again before it is pressed. It is dried slowly over a wood or pine fire, which can leave a faint smoke and keeps the leaf sound enough to age. Then it is packed tight into bamboo baskets and rested in a cool, damp, dark store for one to three years before it is sold.

Liu Bao was made for a market far from home. Chinese miners and labourers in Malaya and across Southeast Asia drank it, above all in the tin mines, and the trade held that it eased the heat and damp of their work and settled the stomach; it was also a taste of home. The tea went by boat down the river to Wuzhou, on to Guangzhou, and out by sea. In the Qing dynasty it was already counted among China’s famous teas.

Liu Bao was made for a market far from home. Chinese miners and labourers in Malaya and across Southeast Asia drank it, above all in the tin mines, and the trade believed it eased the heat and damp of their work and settled the stomach; it was also a taste of home. The tea went by boat down the river to Wuzhou, on to Guangzhou, and out by sea. In the Qing dynasty it was already counted among China’s famous teas.
A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.

Liu Bao that is several decades old is mostly stock that sat in Malaysia or Hong Kong after the mining trade ended. It is prized and hard to date, so the trade reads its age from the basket, the labels and the papers packed with it, and the place it was stored gives each lot its own character.

Mahei names the village in Yiwu. Gushu means “old tree,” the description on this tea’s label. Hong cha, the last two words, means “red tea.” Together the words give a place, a description of the trees and a style of tea.

A section of the old Tea Horse Road passes through Mahei. Ma Zhefeng photographed it while tracing the route through Yiwu. In April 2024, local reporters met Mahei farmer Ding Wanchun picking spring tea with his crew. He said his family needed more than twenty pickers a day.

Huiliu means “returned.” On a Malaysian Returned Liu Bao label, Malaysia names a stop in the life of the tea. Liu Bao made in Guangxi travelled overseas, and older tea later found buyers back in China.

A trade account published in 1951 follows Liu Bao downstream. At Libu the tea changed to a larger wooden boat for Fengkai, then to a powered vessel for Guangzhou. The account names Ipoh and Kuala Lumpur among its final markets.

On a visit to Wuzhou in 2024, Malaysian trade representative Lin Hengyi saw a 1973 import order linking a Malaysian firm and a Wuzhou tea company. His family still kept tea from the 1970s. During the visit, merchants asked him about bringing older Liu Bao back to the Chinese market.

Specialist writing often contrasts Menghai’s strength and bitterness with the gentler reputation of eastern Xishuangbanna. That comparison is a broad regional convention: tree material, craft, blend, age, and storage still create large differences within the county.

The establishment of Menghai Tea Factory and the post-1950 shift toward large-scale production made the county central to twentieth-century Pu’er. Regional leaf increasingly entered factory blends, connecting Menghai with many benchmark raw and ripe productions.
Naka is a village in Mengsong, one of Menghai County’s tea-growing areas.

Menghai County anchors much of western Xishuangbanna’s Pu’er landscape. Names such as Nannuo, Bulang, Mengsong, Hekai, Pasha, and Bada describe distinct mountain areas within the county rather than interchangeable synonyms for Menghai.

In the catalogue for a Malaysian tea fair in 2022, a dark rectangle of pressed tea sits among four cream wrappers printed in red. The exhibitor, Quanyuxuan, offered five Ruigong bricks together at stall 27. The caption identifies that particular offering as ripe tea from 2008, with 250 grams in each brick.

Nanqiao was once the name of the county around Mengzhe in southern Yunnan. Menghai County Nanqiao Tea Company, founded in February 2004, kept that old place name. The China Tea Marketing Association identifies Che Fo Nan as the company’s brand and records that it sold teas in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Southeast Asia.

Tea moved from Yunnan toward Tibet and farther markets along trading networks that are often grouped under the Tea Horse Road. That commerce supported mountain production, market towns, and enduring links between tea-growing communities and distant drinkers.

Pu’er belongs to Yunnan’s long tea history. The name now gathers a family of teas whose identity is tied not only to manufacture, but also to material, place, and the traditions that developed around them.

Modern Pu’er includes sheng and shou. Their processing paths differ, but both sit within a twentieth-century industry that restored tea gardens, expanded production, and developed distinct forms for domestic and export markets.

In 2019 reporters stepped into Wuzhou Tea Factory’s brick-and-timber aging warehouse. Work on it began in 1953, the year the factory opened. Factory staff explained that the porous wooden boards help moderate moisture and temperature while the tea rests after fermentation.

Wuzhou Tea Factory uses handwoven bamboo baskets for its Three Cranes teas. The weave holds its shape and lets air pass through while the tea rests. The supply cooperative describes a network of village weavers, including older residents who earn an income making the baskets.

Wuzhou Tea Factory dates its cold-water piling method to 1958. Workers moisten the leaves and heap them for fermentation. Zhou Mingliang was among the first technicians to practise it. In 1963, Qin Jiquan joined the factory and learned it on shift. When He Meizhen joined the factory in 1988, Qin was one of the senior technicians who taught her.

In July 1959, Guangxi’s trade department circulated an account from tea makers in Buyi, in Cangwu County. Export buyers wanted a brighter, deeper red in the cup and a tighter twist to the leaf. The makers lowered the heat of the firing pan and rolled the leaves more firmly. The circular records how they changed their work in response to buyers overseas.

San He means “Three Cranes.” Wuzhou Tea Factory traces the birds on its trademark to Hegang Tower beside the factory. The works opened for the export trade in 1953. The factory registered the Three Cranes mark in October 1991, nearly four decades later.

Sheng is not given shou’s rapid fermentation. Its character instead changes gradually during storage, with leaf, liquor, aroma, and texture developing over years. Storage conditions therefore belong to the tea’s history, not as a guarantee of quality but as part of how any particular cake has evolved.
Sheng is the undarkened branch of Pu’er, often called raw Pu’er in English. The label distinguishes it from shou, whose accelerated post-fermentation creates a markedly different tea from the outset.

Maocha names an intermediate state in tea production, while sheng describes the tea as it reaches the drinker. Sheng material may be sorted, dried, left loose, or steamed and compressed; the two terms overlap, but they describe the tea from different viewpoints.

After ten years or more, a well-kept ripe pu’er grows smooth and deep, with woody, date-like or medicinal notes the trade calls aged aroma. The leaf keeps changing slowly with the air and moisture around it, which is why storage matters as much as age: dry, clean storage keeps it bright, and damp storage leaves it musty.
Between about five and ten years the pile note has usually aired away. With it gone, the cup turns cleaner and rounder, and its sweetness comes forward.

In its first few years a ripe pu’er often still carries the smell of the pile, a damp, earthy note left over from fermentation that the trade calls pile taste. Air carries it off, so it fades with airing and with time, and a rinse or two before drinking helps.

Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.
From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup.
A smooth, sweet cup with earthy or woody notes. A young ripe tea can carry a faint smell of the pile, which fades with airing or in the first steeps.

Ripe pu’er is pu’er whose leaf is fermented in a warm, damp pile before it is pressed or sold loose. The pile was developed to give, in weeks, the dark and mellow cup that Hong Kong and Guangdong drinkers knew from raw pu’er aged for years. So ripe pu’er is ready to drink soon after it is made, while raw pu’er skips the pile and is usually aged for years.
A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.

In 1973 a team of seven from the Kunming, Menghai and Xiaguan factories went to the Guangzhou tea factory to learn its wet piling. Guangzhou piled with warm water. In Kunming’s cooler, drier air that failed, and Kunming succeeded in 1974 with cold water, sending about ten tonnes to Hong Kong that year. Menghai and Xiaguan each worked out their own ways, and by 1975 Menghai’s method had settled into the ripe pu’er made today.

Before 1949, pu’er already reached Hong Kong and Guangzhou red in the cup. Leaf was packed damp into bamboo baskets, the caravan journey could take a year, and merchants kept the tea for years more before selling it. When faster transport brought fresher tea in the 1950s, those drinkers missed the old taste, and the trade set out to hurry it. In Macau and Hong Kong, Lu Zhuxun sprinkled leaf with water to speed its change. From 1959 the Guangdong tea company in Guangzhou developed a faster fermentation, often blending Yunnan leaf with Guangdong leaf. Yunnan had its own beginnings too: dampening leaf for its pressed jin cha, and in 1958 a steam method at Xiaguan that cut fermentation to about fifteen days.

Most traditional factories still pile on cement floors or in tiled pits, seasoned over years of use; a new floor is first broken in with wetted tea dust until it darkens and stops smelling. Some newer makers pile off the floor on perforated steel to keep the leaf cleaner. A pile can be a hundred kilograms or twenty tonnes, and each maker decides how far to take it: a lighter fermentation keeps some of the raw leaf’s liveliness, a heavier one gives a thicker, darker cup, and taken too far the leaf turns hard and charred.
Ripe pu’er is made by fermenting tea leaves in a damp pile, a process called wet piling.

Ripe pu’er is made by fermenting tea leaves in a damp pile, a process called wet piling. Sun-dried leaf is wetted and heaped so that heat, moisture and microbes can work on it. The heat comes from the microbes themselves, so the pile is covered to hold it in, then turned about once a week to spread it and let air in. It is kept below about 65°C, because hotter than that the leaf starts to char. After one to two months the leaf is dried. Yunnan’s state factories brought the method into production in 1973, after a joint team studied faster piling in Guangdong.

Designer Yin Huize recalled taking hand-painted cartons to the spring Canton Fair with his colleague Tang Zheng. Buyers placed orders from the samples. Tang drew on an openwork jade tiger pendant for the Jixing mark. Yin framed the lettering on the black box with patterns inspired by Chinese lacquerware. The design later appeared on a miniature 15 g carton that airlines gave to passengers.

Much of Yunnan’s loose pu’er once travelled in bulk. In Japan, importers repacked it under their own labels. In 1980, Yunnan brought packaging and tea export designers together so a box could reach a shop counter carrying the province’s own brand. Y562 had Chinese lettering on the front and the English name “Superior Yunnan Pu-erh Tea” on the back. Its companion in the range was Y671, the “little yellow box.”

Y562 is the export code for a loose ripe pu’er from Yunnan. Drinkers nicknamed it the “little black box” after its carton. The Jixing brand mark on the front shows a tiger coming downhill. China Tea’s catalogue lists Y562 in the classic 100 g format.

Pu’er magazine describes the original Y562 blend as grades five and six of ripe tea supplied by Menghai Tea Factory. Its yellow-box companion, Y671, used grades six and seven supplied by Kunming Tea Factory. These grades describe how the leaf was sorted for the original blends.
Pu’er is unusually place-bound for a broad tea family. Yunnan is the central geographic frame, while comparable processing outside the province does not by itself make a tea Yunnan Pu’er.

Regional schemes are editorial aids rather than a single settled ladder. Boundaries, spellings, and the prominence given to one place over another vary, and famous names also function as commercial language. A place label is useful context, not proof of a tea’s exact origin.

Reference maps commonly begin with Xishuangbanna, Pu’er Prefecture, and Lincang, then move toward counties, mountain areas, villages, and local names. Xishuangbanna is often divided into eastern and western tea areas, while other production extends through Yunnan beyond those best-known centers.
